concepts.general_definition: Enhanced Crosslinking and ImmunoPrecipitation (Van Nostrand et al., 2016). A method to map where an RNA-binding protein (RBP) physically contacts RNA inside living cells. The protocol uses UV light to create irreversible covalent bonds between the protein and nearby RNA, then uses an antibody specific to the target RBP to pull down the crosslinked complexes, fragments the RNA, and sequences it. A key feature is that reverse transcription typically stalls and truncates at the crosslink site, so the 5′ end of each read marks the protein–RNA contact point at near-nucleotide resolution. The protocol also generates a size-matched input (SMInput) control alongside the IP experiment.
concepts.project_context: eCLIP is the experimental protocol that produced all the input data in this repository. The architecture overview describes the project as 'an automated parameter optimization system for eCLIP peak calling.' Pre-aligned, deduplicated eCLIP BAM files downloaded from ENCODE serve as the primary inputs to the Snakemake pipeline. The protocol's truncation-at-crosslink property is what makes PureCLIP's crosslink-site signal meaningful. Datasets are identified by RBP and cell line (e.g., RBFOX2_K562), and the repository supports three RBPs across two cell lines.

concepts.general_definition: A protein that binds RNA molecules and regulates their fate — including splicing, export, stability, localization, and translation. RBPs typically recognize specific short sequence motifs in their target RNAs through one or more RNA-binding domains (e.g., RRM, KH domain). The specificity of RBP–RNA interactions makes their binding sites predictable by motif analysis.
concepts.project_context: RBPs are the biological targets whose binding sites this project seeks to identify. The repository focuses on three RBPs: RBFOX2 (a splicing regulator binding the GCAUG motif in introns/3′UTRs), QKI/Quaking (a STAR-family protein binding the bipartite QRE element), and PUM1/Pumilio 1 (binding the Pumilio Response Element to repress translation). Each RBP is treated as a separate dataset. The architecture overview notes that the motif hit-rate scorer measures 'fraction of site windows with a log-odds PWM hit' as a proxy for biological validity — grounded in the idea that genuine RBP binding sites should carry the protein's known sequence motif.

concepts.general_definition: The use of ultraviolet light to create covalent bonds between proteins and nucleic acids at points of direct contact. In CLIP protocols, 254 nm UV irradiates live cells; zero-distance crosslinks form between amino acid residues and bases wherever a protein is physically touching RNA. This 'freezes' transient interactions and allows the complexes to survive the harsh purification steps that follow. The crosslink also introduces a characteristic read truncation during reverse transcription, which is exploited by tools like PureCLIP as the primary signal.
concepts.project_context: UV crosslinking is the biochemical foundation that makes eCLIP data interpretable. The architecture overview notes that 'reverse transcription tends to truncate at the crosslink site, so the 5′ end of the read marks the protein–RNA contact at near-nucleotide resolution.' PureCLIP is specifically designed to model this truncation signal. The postprocessor in workflow/postprocess.py centers each output site on the region summit, preserving the precision that crosslinking provides.

concepts.general_definition: An independent experimental run of the immunoprecipitation step using an antibody specific to the target RBP, performed on separately crosslinked cell lysates. Multiple IP replicates are generated to assess reproducibility: genuine RBP binding sites should appear in all replicates, while noise and off-target signal should not recur. At minimum two replicates are standard for eCLIP.
concepts.project_context: The Snakemake workflow requires at least two IP replicates (validated in pipeline/configs.py). PureCLIP is run both on the merged IP BAM (for final binding site calls) and separately on each per-replicate BAM (to produce per-replicate binding regions). These per-replicate regions are then used by the scorer in run_scorers.py to compute replicate agreement: the fraction of final binding sites that overlap regions called in every individual replicate.

concepts.general_definition: A control library generated in parallel with the eCLIP IP experiment. It follows the same lysis, fragmentation, and sequencing protocol, but without the antibody pulldown step. Because the same size selection is applied, it captures the background distribution of RNA fragments that would be non-specifically retained — the same size range as the genuine IP signal. Dividing or modeling IP signal over SMInput allows removal of background noise.
concepts.project_context: The SMInput BAM is one of the required inputs defined in run_config.yaml under samples.input_control. When the tunable parameter use_input_covariate is set to 1, PureCLIP incorporates the SMInput signal as a covariate in its emission model to suppress non-specific background. This parameter is part of the optimizer's search space, meaning the system learns whether SMInput conditioning improves the composite score for a given dataset.

concepts.general_definition: The computational process of identifying genomic regions that are significantly enriched for sequencing reads relative to a background model. In ChIP-seq, peaks represent protein–DNA binding; in CLIP-seq, peaks represent protein–RNA binding. A peak caller takes aligned BAM files as input and outputs genomic intervals (typically in BED format) that pass a statistical threshold. The quality of peak calls depends heavily on the algorithm's assumptions and its parameter settings.
concepts.project_context: Peak calling is the central computational task that this repository automates and optimizes. The architecture overview defines the project's core purpose as 'an automated parameter optimization system for eCLIP peak calling.' PureCLIP is the peak caller used. The optimizer iterates over parameter sets, re-running the Snakemake DAG (which includes the peak-calling step) each time, and scores the resulting calls against three biological quality signals to find the best configuration.

concepts.general_definition: A peak caller specifically designed for CLIP-seq data (Krakau et al., 2017). Unlike generic ChIP-seq peak callers, PureCLIP models the crosslink-truncation signal through a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) with states representing background, non-enriched, and enriched crosslink activity. It can optionally incorporate an input control BAM as a covariate. Its output includes individual crosslink sites and merged binding regions. Key parameters include bandwidth (smoothing kernel), merge distance (how far apart sites can be and still merge), and a high-precision mode that tightens state transitions.
concepts.project_context: PureCLIP (specifically the pureclip2 fork) is the external peak caller treated as a black box by the repository. It is invoked by the Snakemake workflow (workflow/Snakefile) via the pureclip and pureclip_per_replicate rules. Four of its parameters are tunable by the optimizers: bandwidth_nt [20–100], merge_distance_nt [4–16], high_precision_mode {0,1}, and use_input_covariate {0,1}. The architecture overview notes it is 'not on the default PATH' on the compute VM and must be prepended. The entire optimization loop exists because PureCLIP's ideal parameters are dataset-dependent and cannot be determined analytically.

concepts.general_definition: A probabilistic model where a system is assumed to transition between a finite set of hidden states (which cannot be directly observed) and emit observable outputs at each state. In genomics, HMMs are often applied along a chromosome: each genomic position is assigned to a hidden state (e.g., background, enriched) based on the observed read signal. The Viterbi algorithm finds the most likely hidden state sequence; the forward–backward algorithm computes state probabilities. Parameters include transition probabilities (how often the system changes state) and emission distributions (what signal is expected from each state).
concepts.project_context: PureCLIP uses an HMM internally to model crosslink-site enrichment along the genome, distinguishing enriched binding states from background. The architecture overview describes PureCLIP as 'an HMM-based crosslink-site caller.' This is the reason the bandwidth_nt parameter (which governs the Gaussian smoothing kernel applied to the read signal before HMM decoding) is a critical tunable — it controls how sharply or broadly the emission model resolves peaks.

concepts.general_definition: An individual genomic position identified by a CLIP-seq peak caller as the location where an RBP was UV-crosslinked to RNA. These are point-level calls (single-nucleotide or near-single-nucleotide resolution), arising from the read truncation signal at the crosslink position. Crosslink sites are the finest-grained output of CLIP analysis and are typically merged into binding regions for downstream interpretation.
concepts.project_context: PureCLIP outputs crosslink sites to PureCLIP.crosslink_sites.bed in the results directory. The architecture overview lists this file as one of the Snakemake rule all targets. These raw sites are distinct from the final binding sites: the postprocessor operates on the merged binding_regions.bed, not directly on crosslink_sites.bed. The scoring and optimization pipeline evaluates quality at the binding-region/site level after postprocessing.

concepts.general_definition: A contiguous genomic interval representing a candidate RBP binding site, formed by merging nearby crosslink sites that fall within a specified distance of one another. Binding regions are coarser than individual crosslink sites but more interpretable as functional units. The merge distance parameter controls how aggressively nearby sites are combined.
concepts.project_context: PureCLIP outputs binding regions to PureCLIP.binding_regions.bed. These are produced both for the merged IP run (used for the final binding site calls) and separately for each replicate (used for reproducibility scoring). The BED name field in this file encodes the crosslink events that were merged, stored as semicolon-delimited tokens — a format that postprocess.py parses to apply the min_crosslink_events filter. The merge_distance_nt parameter [4–16] is one of the four PureCLIP tunables in the optimizer's search space.

concepts.general_definition: In molecular biology, 'footprinting' originally referred to the region of DNA or RNA that a bound protein 'protects' from chemical or enzymatic cleavage, producing a blank (footprint) in a gel. In the context of CLIP-seq peak calling, the term has been adapted to refer to normalizing called binding sites to a standardized width that approximates the physical size of the protein's contact area on the RNA — typically a few nucleotides for most RBPs.
concepts.project_context: The architecture overview explicitly references footprinting: 'postprocess.py standardizes raw PureCLIP BED output to a fixed footprint width (~9 nt for these RBPs).' The expected_footprint_width_nt value of 9 nt is stored in priors.json and in run_config.yaml under priors.expected_footprint_width_nt. The postprocessor centers each surviving binding region on its summit and resizes it to force_width (a tunable parameter in [3–15] nt). This normalization ensures all downstream analyses (motif scoring, overlap with references) operate on consistently sized windows.

concepts.general_definition: Steps applied to raw peak-caller output to filter, clean, and normalize the results before downstream analysis. Common postprocessing steps include filtering by minimum read support, merging overlapping intervals, and standardizing site widths. Postprocessing converts tool-specific raw output into a clean, analysis-ready BED file.
concepts.project_context: Postprocessing in this repository is implemented in workflow/postprocess.py. It applies three sequential operations to PureCLIP.binding_regions.bed: (1) filter out regions shorter than min_region_length_nt, (2) filter out regions with fewer than min_crosslink_events crosslink events (parsed from the BED name field), (3) center each surviving region on its summit and resize to force_width. The result is binding_sites.reproducible.bed. Three of the seven tunable parameters belong to this step: min_crosslink_events [2–6], force_width [3–15], and cluster_gap_width [4–16].

concepts.general_definition: A short, recurring sequence pattern in RNA (or its DNA equivalent) that is specifically recognized by an RBP. Motifs are typically 4–12 nucleotides long and can be represented as a consensus string (e.g., UGCAUG for RBFOX2) using IUPAC notation, or more precisely as a Position Weight Matrix (PWM). A binding site is considered motif-bearing if the sequence flanking it contains the expected motif at above-chance frequency.
concepts.project_context: Motif enrichment is one of the three components of the composite objective (weight 0.25 by default). Known motifs for each RBP are stored in priors.json and in the known_motifs list in run_config.yaml. PWM files are organized under data/motifs/{database}/{rbp}/{cell_line}/ in TRANSFAC format. The scorer extracts ±15 nt flanking sequences around each binding site and scores them against all available PWMs, reporting the hit rate of the most enriched motif. RBFOX2's canonical motif is UGCAUG (GCAUG core); QKI's is ACUAAY; PUM1's is UGUANAUA.

concepts.general_definition: A matrix representation of a sequence motif where each row is a position in the motif and each column is a nucleotide (A, C, G, T). Entries contain log-odds scores: log2(observed frequency / background frequency). A positive value means the base is more frequent at that position than expected by chance; a negative value means rarer. To score a candidate sequence, slide the PWM along it and sum the log-odds values at each position. The maximum score over all offsets is the sequence's match score. PWMs are more informative than simple consensus strings because they capture partial matches and position-specific conservation.
concepts.project_context: PWM scoring is implemented in pipeline/motifs.py. The MotifPWM class stores per-position frequency matrices loaded from TRANSFAC files and lazily computes log-odds on first access using: log2((freq + 0.01) / (1 + 4×0.01) / 0.25), with pseudocount 0.01 and uniform background 0.25. A match threshold is derived as min_score + 0.80 × (max_score − min_score). The scorer computes hit rates against both the real binding-site sequences and a composition-matched shuffled background; the reported motif_hit_rate is the foreground rate of the PWM with the highest enrichment (foreground/background ratio). The architecture overview lists 'TRANSFAC/PWM parser, IUPAC regex expansion, scan_sequence_with_pwm() for log-odds scoring' as pipeline/motifs.py's responsibilities.

concepts.general_definition: The logarithm of the ratio of two probabilities: the probability of observing a base given the motif model versus the probability of observing it given background. Using log base 2, the score is in bits. A score of 0 means the base is exactly as likely as background; positive scores indicate enrichment; negative scores indicate depletion. Summing log-odds over all positions of a PWM gives the total motif match score for a window.
concepts.project_context: Log-odds scoring is central to motif analysis in this repository. pipeline/motifs.py computes: log_odds[position][base] = log2((freq / row_total + 0.01) / (1 + 4×0.01) / 0.25). The match_threshold method on MotifPWM expresses the cutoff as a fraction of the PWM's score range (min to max achievable score), at the 80th percentile by default. This threshold approach is robust to negative log-odds values unlike a simple percentage-of-maximum cutoff.

concepts.general_definition: A standardized single-letter code system defined by the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry for representing ambiguous nucleotides in sequence strings. Beyond A, C, G, T, and U, codes include: R=[AG], Y=[CT], M=[AC], K=[GT], W=[AT], S=[GC], N=[ACGT], and several three-base codes (B, D, H, V). Allows compact representation of sequence motifs that tolerate variation at some positions.
concepts.project_context: IUPAC notation is used in two ways in this repository. First, as a fallback motif representation: priors.json and run_config.yaml store consensus strings like TTTGCATGCTT for RBFOX2 motifs using IUPAC codes. Second, pipeline/motifs.py contains an IUPAC_TABLE dict that expands each code to a regex character class (e.g., R → '[AG]'), enabling regex-based motif scanning when no PWM file is available. The scorer falls back to IUPAC regex matching if no PWM files are found for the target protein.

concepts.general_definition: A text file format originally developed for the TRANSFAC database of transcription factor binding sites. Each file describes one motif matrix using tagged lines: 'ID' (motif identifier), 'BF' (biological factor/species), 'P0' (header row listing A, C, G, T), numbered position rows each containing counts or frequencies for the four bases, 'XX' (separator), and '//' (end-of-record). Multiple records can appear in one file.
concepts.project_context: TRANSFAC is the storage format for all PWM motif files in this repository. Files are organized under data/motifs/{database}/{rbp}/{cell_line}/*.transfac and sourced from six databases: mCrossBase, ATtRACT, CISBP-RNA, RBPDB, RBPmap, and oRNAment. The _parse_transfac() function in pipeline/motifs.py reads these files and constructs MotifPWM objects. The scripts/motifs/list_motifs.py and scripts/motifs/reorganize_motifs.py utilities manage this library.

concepts.general_definition: Binary Alignment Map. The standard compressed binary format for storing next-generation sequencing reads after alignment to a reference genome. Each record encodes: chromosome, start position, CIGAR string (describing mismatches and gaps), base qualities, mapping quality, and optional tags. BAM files must be sorted and indexed (.bai) for random access by genomic coordinate. The plain-text equivalent is SAM.
concepts.project_context: BAM files are the primary inputs to the Snakemake pipeline. run_config.yaml specifies paths to pre-aligned, deduplicated BAM files for each IP replicate and the SMInput control under samples.ip and samples.input_control. The workflow's first steps (handled by samtools) index any unindexed BAMs and merge the IP replicates into merged_ip.bam. The architecture overview notes that the repository works 'from pre-aligned, deduplicated BAM files (ENCODE), not raw reads.' Scripts download_data.sh and setup_chr21_bams.sh help acquire and prepare these files.

concepts.general_definition: Browser Extensible Data. A tab-delimited text format for representing genomic intervals. The first three columns (chrom, start, end) are mandatory; optional columns 4–6 are name, score, and strand. Start coordinates are 0-based, end coordinates are exclusive (half-open intervals). BED files are the standard interchange format for genomic peaks, binding sites, and reference annotations.
concepts.project_context: BED files appear at every stage of the pipeline. PureCLIP outputs PureCLIP.crosslink_sites.bed and PureCLIP.binding_regions.bed; postprocess.py writes binding_sites.reproducible.bed; per-replicate regions are stored as ip_{rep}/pureclip_regions.bed and pureclip_sites.bed. The ENCODE reference binding regions and crosslink benchmarks (benchmark.top_regions_bed, benchmark.top_crosslinks_bed) are also BED files. The scorer uses bedtools intersect, shuffle, and getfasta on these files. The load_bed() helper in run_scorers.py reads BED files into pandas DataFrames, keeping only the first six standard columns.

concepts.general_definition: A measure of how consistently binding sites are called across independent experimental replicates. High reproducibility indicates true biological signal; low reproducibility suggests noise or technical artifacts. Raw replicate agreement (fraction of sites overlapping all replicates) is inflated by large, broad intervals that overlap by geometric chance, so it requires correction.
concepts.project_context: Reproducibility is the highest-weighted term (0.5) in the composite objective. The repository implements two reproducibility metrics. Raw replicate_agreement: fraction of final binding sites (binding_sites.reproducible.bed) overlapping the per-replicate PureCLIP binding regions from every replicate, computed via chained bedtools intersect -u calls. Chance-corrected reproducibility_score: (observed − expected) / (1 − expected), clamped to [0, 1], where expected is the mean agreement over three random shuffles of the binding sites (each site relocated within its own chromosome by bedtools shuffle -chrom, preserving chromosome-level density). The architecture overview explicitly states this correction ensures reproducibility 'cannot be inflated by keeping only a few broad sites.'

concepts.general_definition: A statistical adjustment that removes the portion of an agreement measure attributable to random overlap. Without correction, a caller that returns a small number of very broad intervals can achieve high apparent reproducibility simply because broad intervals are more likely to overlap by chance. The correction subtracts the expected agreement under a random null model and rescales the result: (observed − expected) / (1 − expected). This is analogous in spirit to Cohen's kappa for categorical agreement.
concepts.project_context: Chance correction is implemented in the replicate_reproducibility() function in scorers/run_scorers.py. The null model is built by shuffling the binding sites with bedtools shuffle -chrom (intervals randomized within their own chromosome, preserving per-chromosome count and interval length) and re-measuring agreement. This is repeated three times (n_shuffles=3) and the mean is taken as expected. The final reproducibility_score feeds into the composite objective with weight 0.5. The architecture overview describes this explicitly: 'Not gameable by keeping a few broad intervals.'

concepts.general_definition: A large, ongoing international consortium project (NIH-funded) that systematically maps functional elements in the human genome, including transcription factor binding sites, histone modifications, chromatin accessibility, and RNA-binding protein binding sites from CLIP-seq experiments. ENCODE provides standardized, publicly available datasets for cell lines including K562 and HepG2, and releases curated high-confidence binding region sets.
concepts.project_context: ENCODE serves two roles in this repository. First, all input BAM files are sourced from ENCODE (pre-aligned, deduplicated eCLIP data; downloaded via download_data.sh). Second, ENCODE's curated high-confidence binding regions are used as a benchmark ground truth: the benchmark.top_regions_bed and benchmark.top_crosslinks_bed paths in run_config.yaml point to ENCODE reference BED files. The scorer computes benchmark_region_recall as the fraction of these reference regions recovered by the current parameter set, contributing 0.25 to the composite objective.

concepts.general_definition: In the context of peak calling evaluation, recall (also called sensitivity) is the fraction of known positive regions that are recovered by the caller: true_positives / (true_positives + false_negatives). A benchmark set of curated reference regions acts as the ground truth. High recall means the caller finds most of the known sites; low recall means it misses them, often because filtering is too stringent.
concepts.project_context: Benchmark recall is the third component of the composite objective (weight 0.25). The scorer computes it as: (ENCODE reference regions with ≥1 overlap in binding_sites.reproducible.bed) / (total reference regions on analyzed chromosomes). When learn_on_chr21=true is set, the recall is restricted to chr21 reference regions only — otherwise the genome-wide reference set would cap recall at ~4.5%, making the signal uninterpretable. The recall term is critical as a guard against site collapse: an optimizer that discards real sites to inflate reproducibility will see recall drop.

concepts.general_definition: A single scalar metric formed by combining multiple quality signals into a weighted average, used as the target for an optimization algorithm. A composite objective is necessary when no single metric fully captures the desired outcome — in eCLIP analysis, reproducibility alone can be gamed by collapsing to a few broad sites, motif rate alone can be gamed by keeping only trivially motif-rich regions, and recall alone can be gamed by keeping everything. Combining all three with appropriate weights and safeguards creates a more honest signal.
concepts.project_context: The composite objective is the single source of truth that both optimizers maximize. Implemented in agentic_pureclip.scoring.objective::composite_objective(), it is also imported directly by the dashboard API (dashboard/api/collectors.py) so the dashboard always reflects the live formula. The formula is: composite = weighted_average(reproducibility × 0.5, motif × 0.25, recall × 0.25) × min(1, n_binding_sites / 10). Weights are renormalized over whichever terms are present in the score report. The yield_factor = min(1, n_sites / 10) is the collapse guard: below 10 sites the score ramps linearly toward zero. Weights are configurable via priors.json.

concepts.general_definition: A penalty term in an optimization objective that prevents a degenerate solution where the algorithm maximizes quality metrics by drastically reducing the number of output sites. With very few sites, reproducibility and motif hit rate trivially approach 1.0 (a handful of hand-picked perfect sites), producing a falsely high score. A yield factor multiplier ramps the objective toward zero when site count is too low.
concepts.project_context: The collapse guard was added after a 12-hour run observed Optuna collapsing QKI to 1 site for a composite score of 0.78. The yield_factor is implemented in agent/decisions.py::yield_factor(): min(1.0, max(0, n_binding_sites) / DEFAULT_MIN_SITES), where DEFAULT_MIN_SITES=10. At fewer than 10 sites the composite is scaled down proportionally; at 10 or more it has no effect. The LLM prompt explicitly warns: 'Below 10 sites the score is ramped toward zero, so a handful of perfect sites is NOT a win.' The recall term also serves as a natural anti-collapse signal because discarding sites reduces recall.

concepts.general_definition: An immortalized population of cells derived from a specific tissue and grown continuously in culture. Cell lines are used in molecular biology as reproducible, scalable experimental models. Different cell lines express different genes and proteins, so the same RBP can exhibit different binding landscapes across cell lines. ENCODE tier-1 cell lines (K562, HepG2) are prioritized because they have the most comprehensive reference data.
concepts.project_context: Two cell lines appear in this repository's datasets. K562 is a human chronic myelogenous leukemia line; HepG2 is a human hepatocellular carcinoma/liver line. Both are ENCODE tier-1. Datasets are named by RBP and cell line (e.g., RBFOX2_K562, RBFOX2_HepG2, QKI_K562, QKI_HepG2, PUM1_K562). The cell line is a field in run_config.yaml and is used by the scorer to select the appropriate PWM files from data/motifs/{database}/{rbp}/{cell_line}/. The architecture overview notes that RBFOX2_K562 is 'the hardest dataset (reproducibility ~0.10)' and is the main scientific focus.

concepts.general_definition: A common strategy in genomics tool development and parameter tuning where analysis is restricted to a single, well-annotated chromosome to dramatically reduce runtime while preserving a representative signal. Chromosome 21 is frequently chosen because it is the smallest human autosome, making it fast to process, yet contains a representative range of gene types and regulatory elements.
concepts.project_context: chr21 fast mode is controlled by the pureclip.learn_on_chr21 boolean in run_config.yaml. When enabled, PureCLIP is run only on chromosome 21, reducing runtime from hours (full genome) to minutes per iteration. The architecture overview notes this as '~minutes/iter instead of hours; used for all batch experiments.' Because recall is computed against ENCODE reference regions, the scorer automatically restricts the reference BED to chr21 when this mode is active, preventing an artificially low recall cap (~4.5% for genome-wide reference on chr21-only calls). Scripts setup_chr21_bams.sh and extract_chromosome.sh prepare chr21-subsetted BAMs.

concepts.general_definition: A Python-based workflow management system for bioinformatics pipelines. Workflows are defined as rules, each specifying input files, output files, and a shell or Python command. Snakemake automatically infers the execution order as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) from file dependencies, only re-runs rules whose outputs are missing or out of date, and supports parallelism and cluster execution.
concepts.project_context: Snakemake is the workflow engine that runs the bioinformatics pipeline in workflow/Snakefile. It defines rules for indexing BAMs, merging IP replicates, running PureCLIP on the merged and per-replicate BAMs, postprocessing, and scoring. The evaluate_config() function in agent/evaluation.py invokes Snakemake programmatically via pipeline/runner.py, always forcing the pureclip, pureclip_per_replicate, and postprocess rules to re-execute (via --forcerun) so that parameter changes take effect even when upstream files are unchanged.

concepts.general_definition: The component of a peak-calling optimization pipeline responsible for quantifying the quality of a given set of binding sites against independent biological evidence. A well-designed scorer combines multiple orthogonal signals so the optimizer cannot satisfy all criteria simultaneously by gaming any one metric.
concepts.project_context: scorers/run_scorers.py is the quality-assessment layer invoked at the end of each Snakemake DAG run. It computes three metrics — chance-corrected replicate agreement (reproducibility_score), motif hit rate (fraction of sites bearing a PWM-matched sequence), and benchmark recall (fraction of ENCODE reference regions recovered) — and writes them along with the parameters that produced them to score_report.json. The architecture overview notes that score_report.json is 'self-describing: includes the params that produced it,' enabling historical re-scoring when the objective formula changes.
